title: Home heat kit
summary: What a household needs to stay warm and safe when the furnace or the power is out.

items.text: Carbon monoxide alarms that run on batteries or have battery backup, on every level and outside each sleeping area
items.note: Put one near the area you heat with a fireplace, wood stove or kerosene heater. Test monthly.

items.text: Smoke alarms, including one near the area you heat
Multipurpose (A-B-C) dry-chemical fire extinguisher, kept near the heat source
At least one emergency heat source, such as a fireplace or wood stove vented to the outside
items.note: CDC: combustion heaters only if properly vented. Kerosene and propane space heaters are not vented: see Kerosene and propane heaters for the only conditions to run one. Never an oven, gas range, grill or camp stove. Have the chimney inspected each year.

items.text: Plenty of dry, seasoned firewood, if you heat with wood
Delivered heating fuel (oil, propane) refilled before you run low
items.note: Refill before you run out: deliveries may not reach you for days after a winter storm.

items.text: Fuel in containers made and labelled for it, stored outside the house
items.note: Kerosene in its own can, never one that held gasoline. See Store fuel safely.

items.text: Metal ash container with a lid
Extra warm clothing: layers, long underwear, socks, slippers and hats
Wearable blankets or extra sleep layers for any baby
items.note: No loose blankets in a baby’s sleep area.

items.text: Plastic to cover windows from the inside, and towels or rags for the cracks under doors
Flashlights or battery lanterns, with extra batteries
items.note: Not candles, and never a fuel lantern indoors.

items.text: Propylene-glycol antifreeze for drain traps, if you may have to drain the house

sources.name: CDC, Preparing for a Winter Storm (last reviewed December 2, 2025)
sources.used: Smoke detector and battery-operated CO detector near the area heated by a fireplace, wood stove or kerosene heater, test monthly; multipurpose dry-chemical fire extinguisher nearby; chimney inspected each year; easy-to-read indoor thermometer; cover windows with plastic from the inside

sources.name: CDC, Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm (last reviewed August 25, 2026)
sources.used: At least one heat source; a fireplace up to code with plenty of dry firewood; vented to the outside; turning on the stove for heat is not safe; towels or rags in cracks under doors

sources.name: US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), Carbon Monoxide Questions and Answers, as checked in surv-carbon-monoxide
sources.used: Battery-operated or battery-backup CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas

sources.name: National Weather Service, Prepare! Don't Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise
sources.used: Flashlight and extra batteries; battery-powered radio; heating fuel, refuel before you are empty, carriers may not reach you for days; emergency heat source properly ventilated; fire extinguisher, smoke alarm, test monthly

sources.name: FEMA, Keep Warm During a Winter Power Outage and Avoid Hypothermia (January 18, 2018)
sources.used: Extra clothing, blankets or sleeping bags

sources.name: National Institute on Aging (NIH), Hypothermia: A Cold Weather Risk for Older People (January 16, 2009)
sources.used: Long underwear, socks and slippers, hat indoors

sources.name: Safe to Sleep (NICHD, NIH), Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk
sources.used: Wearable blanket or an extra layer instead of blankets in the sleep area

sources.name: American Red Cross, news article on extreme cold safety steps (February 20, 2025)

sources.name: US Fire Administration, Fireplace and Wood Stove Safety (card)
